the attached research plan defines the intended study and supplies literature leads. verify its factual claims and references. this prompt governs execution: keep the core comparison fixed, but choose the mechanistic methods and discovery direction yourself. do not assume the expected findings are true.

Gemma-IT is a same-family, same-size aligned reference, not the direct training parent of GaMS-Instruct. endpoint differences cannot establish what Slovene continual pretraining, instruction tuning, or the small safety-training set caused.

step 1 - explore and establish feasibility. load both original models, pin revisions, verify their official tokenizers and chat templates, and inspect behavior and activations on a small development set in both languages. check coherent output, baseline refusal, and hidden-state extraction. use text-only inputs and comparable precision and inference settings; record unavoidable differences. inspect where the models behave similarly and where they differ, without committing to a mechanism. estimate the compute needed before scaling up. use separate smoke-test data and keep final evaluation untouched. if an edit fails or destroys language ability, investigate and report the failure rather than quietly substituting another model or calling incoherence successful refusal suppression.

step 2 - find the scientific opening. develop 5–7 distinct, falsifiable explanations or research directions from the pilot and the literature. search beyond refusal-vector papers, including multilingual representations, decision calibration, causal intervention, and capability interference. actively try to disprove novelty by reading the closest primary sources. select one or two promising directions for deeper experiments.

possible starting points: does cross-language intervention transfer depend on something that direction cosine misses? can we distinguish loss of harmfulness information from a changed mapping between that information and refusal? does interference with language-relevant computation explain different utility costs? these are suggestions, not required findings or an exhaustive menu. replace them if the evidence points somewhere better.

for each selected hypothesis, state its prediction, strongest competing explanation, simplest baseline, and a result that would falsify it. discovering that familiar geometry fails to predict behavior can be valuable if you establish its boundary. merely applying Heretic to GaMS, observing EN–SL vector similarity, or finding separable harmfulness after refusal declines is insufficient by itself as a novelty claim. if an exploratory hypothesis fails the novelty check, replace that hypothesis while preserving the core study.

step 3 - freeze the data and intervention protocol. separate Heretic construction/optimization data, mechanistic development data, held-out mechanistic validation, and final behavioral evaluation. keep translations, paraphrases, and harmful/harmless counterparts from the same semantic source together when splitting. audit overlap by source and meaning, not only exact strings. Heretic's default sources and Semantic-Harmful/Semantic-Harmless may overlap; those pairs cannot automatically serve as independent validation.

create one main Heretic checkpoint per original model using the same pinned version, English prompt source, comparable objectives, and equal search budgets. choose checkpoints by a declared development-only rule balancing refusal reduction and harmless divergence. evaluate that same English-derived edit in both languages. a community Gemma edit is a sanity reference, not a substitute for the matched main intervention. record configurations, seeds, selected trials, precision, and checkpoint hashes. distinguish differences in achieved optimization from intrinsic model properties. additional seeds or edit strengths may support a focused robustness analysis, but keep them separate from the four core checkpoints.

step 4 - measure behavior and utility. use the official NASK-PIB/RefusEU evaluation data for English and Slovene, following its published scoring protocol where reproducible. report harmful compliance/attack success, refusal, and language consistency separately. refusal and harmful compliance are not complements: ambiguous, irrelevant, malformed, and empty outputs need explicit treatment. include a small independent benign safety-adjacent set to measure over-refusal. a model that refuses everything, or cannot answer coherently, must not look successful.

use the same frozen judge and rubric across conditions, with model identity hidden. check scoring sensitivity using a second independent judge on a stratified sample. prepare a blinded EN/SL sample for human review; if qualified human review is unavailable, mark it pending and state the limitation instead of claiming it happened.

for utility, use Slovenian LLM Eval and the corresponding English tasks: ARC-Challenge, BoolQ, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PIQA, and Winogrande. report individual tasks and their macro-average, emphasizing original-to-edited changes within each language. also measure harmless divergence on held-out inputs, wrong-language output, repetition, and output validity. Heretic's optimization KL alone is not independent evidence of preserved utility.

do not assume RefusEU examples sharing an ID are exact translations, or that EN and SL benchmark difficulty is identical. verify correspondence before making paired cross-language claims. use a separate faithful EN/SL contrast set for controlled language comparisons. translate only missing material, preserve semantic IDs, document translation checks, and distinguish automated checks from native-speaker review. published model-card scores are context and sanity checks; measure the four checkpoints yourself under the same protocol.

step 5 - connect representations to behavior. complete the mechanistic core: layer-wise bilingual harmful/harmless direction characterization in both originals, and held-out harmfulness separability before and after Heretic. choose and justify activation locations and token positions. select layers, probes, and hyperparameters on development data only.

control for topic, wording, prompt length, language identity, and response leakage. decoding harmfulness from generated refusal text is not evidence that a pre-response harmfulness signal drives refusal. compare a frozen original-model probe with appropriately cross-validated probes refitted after editing where useful: failure of the frozen probe can reflect representation drift rather than information loss. do not interpret raw cross-model vector cosine as shared mechanism without establishing comparable coordinates.

relate internal measurements to actual behavioral changes in each language. high probe accuracy establishes decodability, not causal use. a harmful-minus-harmless direction is only refusal-associated until interventions support a stronger interpretation. changes in a direction directly targeted by Heretic are expected and cannot alone carry the discovery.

step 6 - pursue the strongest explanation. use the freedom from step 2 to design the smallest decisive experiment. where justified, extract EN- and SL-derived directions and test the source-language × evaluation-language transfer matrix within each model. choose intervention locations and strengths on development data, and include no-op and matched random-direction controls plus benign utility checks. keep these activation interventions separate from the main Heretic comparison.

you may instead pursue subspaces, layer-specific interventions, representation-to-action coupling, or another approach supported by the pilot. the goal is a result that distinguishes competing explanations and predicts something on untouched data. use held-out semantic categories or an independent prompt source to challenge it. explain what survives, what breaks, and where the claim stops. prefer one well-tested insight over a large collection of loosely connected metrics. preserve the behavioral and mechanistic core even if every novelty candidate fails.

step 7 - test the claims honestly. freeze primary outcomes and confirmatory analyses before final evaluation. report original-to-edited effects for each model and language, with effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals. compare those changes across models and languages without attributing them to a specific training stage.

state the resampling and aggregation units. pair outputs on the same prompts and cluster translations/paraphrases by underlying semantic item; use cross-language pairing only where correspondence is established. four checkpoints, many layers, or many prompts do not create many independent model families. prompt-level uncertainty also does not measure variation across Heretic optimization runs. account for searching across hypotheses and layers, separate exploratory from confirmatory results, and state when sample sizes cannot resolve a difference. if resources require subsampling, freeze a stratified sample before viewing results and narrow the claims accordingly.

bonus - examine cjvt/GaMS3-12B as a bounded pre-instruction diagnostic. test harmfulness separability and a small EN/SL behavior sample with appropriate base-model formatting. do not compare its raw refusal rate with chat models as if the tasks were identical. only attempt base abliteration if refusal-like behavior is reproducible, the intervention has an interpretable target, and it does not jeopardize the main study. intermediate training checkpoints and no-safety training controls belong to a later extension unless already available.

deliver a reproducible repository and a paper grounded in executed experiments: pinned dependencies, split manifests, configurations, per-example outputs and scores, analysis scripts, and figures covering the four checkpoints in both languages. distinguish observations, interpretations, failed hypotheses, and unexecuted proposals. recompute every headline number from saved results and reconcile the abstract, tables, figures, and conclusions after the final audit. the discovery may change as evidence accumulates; the final paper must reflect the strongest claim that actually survives.

Over-refusal rate is the fraction of benign-prompt responses classified as refused. Language consistency is verified by GlotLID \\citep{Kargaran2023}.\n\n\\paragraph{Generation truncation.} The 256-token generation limit truncates a large share of edited English outputs: 95.4\\% of Gemma-edit EN and 94.2\\% of GaMS3-edit EN responses are truncated, compared with 96.7\\% for Gemma-orig EN and 26.3\\% for GaMS3-orig EN. Slovene truncation rates are lower (69.8\\% for Gemma-edit SL, 92.1\\% for GaMS3-edit SL). The high English truncation rate means that many compliant English responses were cut short, and the judge classified their refusal status from incomplete text.\n\n\\paragraph{Judge certification.} The Qwen3-14B workhorse judge was calibrated against GPT-4.1 labels on a held-out panel. English certification passed: unweighted $\\kappa = 0.86$ $[0.77, 0.92]$, gate met. Slovene certification failed: unweighted $\\kappa = 0.72$ $[0.63, 0.81]$, below the $0.80$ threshold. All Slovene absolute rates therefore carry a measurement caveat. Relative comparisons within Slovene (e.g., orig vs.\\ edit) are less affected, since the judge bias is approximately constant across checkpoints.\n\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{Refusal Suppression Across Languages}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:headline} and Figure~\\ref{fig:refusal-rates} report the main refusal evaluation. Abliteration produces dramatically different cross-lingual outcomes for the two models.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Refusal rate and attack success rate (ASR) on RefusEU S5 harmful prompts ($n=280$ per cell), with 95\\% Clopper--Pearson confidence intervals. Over-refusal is on S6 benign prompts ($n=150$). Edited English outputs are truncated at 256 tokens in 94--95\\% of cases (see Method).}\n\\label{tab:headline}\n\\begin{tabular}{llccc}\n\\toprule\nCheckpoint & Lang & Refusal & ASR & Over-refusal \\\\\n\\midrule\nGaMS3-orig & EN & .986 [.971,.996] & .015 [.004,.030] & .100 [.053,.153] \\\\\nGaMS3-orig & SL & .871 [.829,.907] & .012 [.000,.027] & .107 [.060,.160] \\\\\nGaMS3-edit & EN & .014 [.004,.029] & .982 [.964,.996] & .000 [.000,.000] \\\\\nGaMS3-edit & SL & .000 [.000,.000] & .972 [.952,.992] & .000 [.000,.000] \\\\\n\\midrule\nGemma-orig & EN & .971 [.950,.989] & .026 [.007,.049] & .087 [.040,.133] \\\\\nGemma-orig & SL & .939 [.911,.964] & .016 [.004,.031] & .327 [.253,.400] \\\\\nGemma-edit & EN & .287 [.233,.341] & .738 [.681,.794] & .013 [.000,.033] \\\\\nGemma-edit & SL & .739 [.686,.786] & .103 [.067,.143] & .193 [.133,.260] \\\\\n\\midrule\nCommunity-ref & EN & .054 [.029,.082] & 1.00 [1.00,1.00] & .007 [.000,.020] \\\\\nCommunity-ref & SL & .114 [.079,.154] & .870 [.822,.909] & .027 [.007,.053] \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\textbf{GaMS3}: Abliteration removes refusal almost completely in both languages. English refusal drops from 98.6\\% to 1.4\\% (McNemar $p < 10^{-81}$); Slovene refusal drops from 87.1\\% to 0.0\\% ($p < 10^{-73}$). Over-refusal also drops to zero in both languages. The edit transfers fully.\n\n\\textbf{Gemma}: Abliteration partially suppresses English refusal (97.1\\% $\\to$ 28.7\\%, $p < 10^{-57}$) but barely affects Slovene (93.9\\% $\\to$ 73.9\\%, $p < 10^{-15}$). The English ASR reaches only 73.8\\%, far below GaMS3's 98.2\\%. In Slovene, Gemma-edit's ASR is 10.3\\%; the edit scarcely works.\n\n\\textbf{Community reference}: The independently abliterated Gemma achieves much lower refusal in both English (5.4\\%) and Slovene (11.4\\%), suggesting that a more thorough abliteration procedure can reach deeper into the refusal mechanism even for Gemma.\n\nThe keyword counter that verified both the Gemma-edit and GaMS3-edit checkpoints did not detect this divergence. Both checkpoints were selected by the same fallback rule (minimise keyword refusals), and neither reached the primary gate. The next section quantifies why.\n\n\\subsection{Keyword Measurement Bias}\n\\label{sec:keyword-bias}\n\nThe keyword refusal counter that Heretic uses as its primary objective counts English refusal phrases (``I cannot'', ``I'm sorry'', etc.) in model responses. This counter is structurally unable to detect Slovene refusals, which are expressed in Slovene. The consequence is not merely that the optimiser misses a signal; the verified checkpoints cannot serve as language-neutral references for refusal evaluation.\n\nWe quantify the bias using the language-gap score $\\Delta_{\\mathrm{lang}}$. For each language $\\ell$, let $d_\\ell = r^\\mathrm{kw}_\\ell - r^\\mathrm{judge}_\\ell$ be the difference between the keyword positive rate and the judge positive rate. The language-gap score is $\\Delta_{\\mathrm{lang}} = d_{\\mathrm{SL}} - d_{\\mathrm{EN}}$: the excess understatement of refusal by the keyword counter in Slovene relative to English. For the Gemma-edit checkpoint on a verified subset of 100 paired S5 prompts ($n=100$, Qwen reference channel): the keyword counter fires on 87\\% of English responses but on 0\\% of Slovene responses, while the reference judge finds 13\\% English refusal and 82\\% Slovene refusal. Thus $d_{\\mathrm{SL}} = 0.00 - 0.82 = -0.82$ and $d_{\\mathrm{EN}} = 0.87 - 0.13 = 0.74$:\n\n\\begin{equation}\n\\Delta_{\\mathrm{lang}} = d_{\\mathrm{SL}} - d_{\\mathrm{EN}} = -0.82 - 0.74 = -1.56 \\quad [95\\% \\text{ CI: } -1.68, -1.44]\n\\end{equation}\n\nFigure~\\ref{fig:keyword-bias} illustrates the gap. The negative sign of $\\Delta_{\\mathrm{lang}}$ indicates that the keyword counter understates refusal in Slovene far more than in English: in Slovene the counter detects nothing while the judge finds 82\\% refusal, whereas in English the counter over-fires at 87\\% against a judge rate of only 13\\%.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_2_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Keyword counter vs.\\ reference judge positive rates for the Gemma-edit checkpoint on 100 verified paired prompts. The keyword counter fires on 87\\% of English responses but 0\\% of Slovene responses; the reference judge finds 13\\% English refusal and 82\\% Slovene refusal. $\\Delta_{\\mathrm{lang}} = d_{\\mathrm{SL}} - d_{\\mathrm{EN}} = -1.56$ [$-1.68$, $-1.44$]. The annotation shows TBF $= 1.0$: 6/6 Gemma and 37/37 GaMS3 candidates invisible to the keyword objective are counted by the keyword-based scorer C; under the reference judge J, the counts are 5/5 and 6/6.}\n  \\label{fig:keyword-bias}\n\\end{figure}\n\nThe \\textbf{threshold-blind fraction} (TBF) quantifies the consequence for optimiser selection. TBF is the share of candidates that a scorer places at or below the selection threshold ($\\leq 10/100$ refusals) but the keyword objective places above it. In both searches, TBF $= 1.0$. This follows mechanically from the keyword floors: the minimum keyword count across all 116 candidates was 72 for Gemma and 16 for GaMS3, both above the 10-refusal selection threshold. Since no candidate's keyword count is $\\leq 10$, every candidate that any other scorer would select is invisible to the keyword objective. Under the keyword-based scorer C, 6 out of 6 eligible Gemma candidates and 37 out of 37 eligible GaMS3 candidates are invisible; under the reference judge J, the counts are 5 out of 5 and 6 out of 6.\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:keyword} summarises the keyword counter's behaviour across four evaluation conditions, computed on held-out prompts from both Heretic searches (first-100-token window; $n$ ranges from 70 to 490 depending on condition). On edited English text, 81\\% of the keyword counter's refusal detections are false positives---keyword fragments appearing in compliant responses---confirming that the counter both over-fires in English and is silent in Slovene.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Keyword refusal counter vs.\\ judge reference on held-out prompts. The keyword counter correctly identifies English refusals in unedited models (CONCORDANT) but produces zero positives on Slovene text (SILENT) and misfires on edited English text (MISFIRING, FP share 0.81).}\n\\label{tab:keyword}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccccl}\n\\toprule\nCondition & $n$ & $\\kappa$ & KW pos.\\ rate & Ref.\\ base rate & Mechanism \\\\\n\\midrule\nOriginal EN & 70 & 0.20 & 0.94 & 0.94 & CONCORDANT \\\\\nOriginal SL & 70 & 0.00 & 0.00 & 0.96 & SILENT \\\\\nEdited EN & 490 & 0.02 & 0.34 & 0.17 & MISFIRING \\\\\nEdited SL & 490 & 0.00 & 0.00 & 0.44 & SILENT \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\subsection{Depth Placement vs.\\ Dose}\n\\label{sec:placement}\n\nAbliteration edits a subset of the model's transformer layers. The Heretic optimiser treats which layers to edit and the scaling coefficient as free parameters, producing candidates that vary in both \\emph{where} the edit energy is placed (depth placement) and \\emph{how much} total energy is applied (dose, measured as the Frobenius norm of the weight perturbation). We ask whether placement matters independently of dose.\n\n\\paragraph{Causal write profiles.} For each model, we construct a \\emph{causal write profile} by applying single-layer abliteration edits to each of the model's transformer layers in isolation, then measuring the residual refusal rate. This profile reveals which layers, when edited alone, are most effective at suppressing refusal. The \\emph{write-profile overlap} $O_{\\mathrm{SL}}$ measures the energy-normalised alignment between a multi-layer candidate's edit distribution and the causal write profile: higher overlap means the candidate concentrates its energy on layers that matter.\n\nFor Gemma, the confirmation-level Spearman correlations between the write-profile overlap and residual refusal are $\\rho = -0.96$ for English and $\\rho = -0.83$ for Slovene ($n = 18$ weight cells). The English and Slovene profiles are correlated at $\\rho = 0.59$. For GaMS3, the profile is analysed through a factorial design with two energy levels (E2 and E3) and ten placement configurations. The Spearman correlation between write-profile overlap $O_{\\mathrm{SL}}$ and residual Slovene refusal is $\\rho = -0.90$ ($p < 10^{-7}$), holding within both energy levels ($\\rho = -0.97$ at E2, $\\rho = -0.95$ at E3).\n\n\\paragraph{Replication in Qwen3-8B.} The write-profile overlap $O$ replicates in a third model, Qwen3-8B, with Spearman $\\rho = -0.76$ (pooled), $-0.93$ (E2), and $-0.84$ (E3), across 9 out of 9 matched groups. The overlap metric transfers: the rank ordering of which layers matter generalises beyond the two models in the primary study.\n\n\\paragraph{Primary criterion: falsified.} The primary criterion asks whether placement explains variance in residual refusal beyond dose. Adding placement to a dose-only regression yields $\\Delta R^2 = 0.027$ (Gemma) and $\\Delta R^2 = 0.056$ (GaMS3): placement contributes negligibly once dose is controlled. At the keyword floor---the region of the search space the optimiser actually selects from---dose dominates ($p = 0.774$). The within-model correlations between overlap and refusal, though strong, reflect the confounding of placement with dose across the search space rather than an independent causal contribution.\n\n\\paragraph{Raw depth.} Raw depth of the edit (mean edited layer index) does not significantly predict residual Slovene refusal in GaMS3: Spearman $\\rho = -0.34$, $p = 0.15$ (Figure~\\ref{fig:depth-placement}b). The write-profile overlap, which accounts for the non-uniform importance of layers, is the informative predictor (Figure~\\ref{fig:depth-placement}a).\n\n\\paragraph{Cross-model prediction.} The frozen activation-space DEV index---a single depth summary computed on Gemma and applied without refit to Qwen3-8B---fails cross-model prediction entirely: Spearman $\\rho = -0.009$ over 21 pooled cells (item-bootstrap 95\\% CI $[-0.13, 0.19]$, permutation $p = 0.16$). This failure concerns the frozen index, not the write-profile concept itself, which replicates (see above).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_3_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Residual Slovene refusal rate for GaMS3-12B-Instruct as a function of two predictors. (a)~Write-profile overlap $O_{\\mathrm{SL}}$: Spearman $\\rho = -0.90$ ($p < 10^{-7}$); within energy levels, $\\rho = -0.97$ (E2) and $\\rho = -0.95$ (E3). Higher overlap with the causal write profile predicts lower residual refusal. (b)~Raw depth of the edit (mean edited layer index): Spearman $\\rho = -0.34$, $p = 0.15$ (not significant). Raw depth alone does not predict residual refusal; the overlap metric, which accounts for layer importance, is the informative predictor.}\n  \\label{fig:depth-placement}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\n\\paragraph{Evaluation validity.} The keyword measurement bias is the central finding of this study. Abliterated checkpoints verified only by an English keyword counter carry no information about non-English refusal behaviour. The keyword counter detected zero Slovene refusals across all conditions (0/490 held-out Slovene responses, 0/100 verified Gemma-edit Slovene responses), and its threshold-blind fraction was 1.0 in both searches. TBF $= 1.0$ follows from the keyword floors (72 and 16, both above the 10-refusal threshold) combined with the counter's 81\\% false-positive rate on edited English text: the counter simultaneously over-fires in the source language and is silent in the target language. Any downstream use of these checkpoints as language-neutral references for safety evaluation inherits this validity gap.\n\n\\paragraph{Depth placement.} The depth placement finding has a narrower scope. Within a single model, the write-profile overlap $O_{\\mathrm{SL}}$---the energy-normalised alignment between a candidate's edit distribution and the causal write profile---correlates strongly with residual Slovene refusal, and this pattern replicates in Qwen3-8B ($\\rho = -0.76/-0.93/-0.84$, 9/9 matched groups). However, the primary criterion was falsified: placement does not explain variance beyond dose ($\\Delta R^2$ of 0.027 and 0.056). At the keyword floor, dose dominates ($p = 0.774$). The frozen DEV index, a single depth summary applied across models without refit, fails entirely ($\\rho = -0.009$). The practical consequence is that while the write-profile concept transfers, no fixed depth prescription carries from one model to another, and depth gains little once dose is held constant.\n\n\\paragraph{Judge reliability.} The depth-placement experiment's own judge (exp12) missed its certification gate ($\\kappa = 0.683$), adding a measurement caveat to the placement results beyond the main study's Slovene caveat ($\\kappa = 0.72$).\n\n\\paragraph{Model divergence.} The GaMS3--Gemma contrast is striking: the edit transfers fully to GaMS3 but largely fails on Gemma. We observe this asymmetry but do not attribute it to a specific mechanism. The two checkpoints differ in their training data (GaMS3 was continually pretrained on 140B tokens including Slovene \\citep{Vres2026}), but we study only two models from one architecture family, so we cannot isolate whether continual pretraining, the specific training mix, or some other factor drives the difference.\n\n\\subsection{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\nSeveral limitations constrain the scope of these findings.\n", "numLines": 200, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 223}}

<body>

<a class="skip-link" href="#main-content">Skip to main content</a>

<nav class="section-nav" aria-label="Section navigation">
  <ol>
    <li><a href="#hero">Overview</a></li>
    <li><a href="#contributions">Contributions</a></li>
    <li><a href="#method">Method</a></li>

<main id="main-content">

  <!-- HERO -->
  <section class="hero" id="hero">
    <h1>An English Keyword Objective Is Blind to Its Own Edit in Slovene</h1>

    <p class="tldr">
      Abliteration removes refusal from language models by orthogonalising weights
      against an English-extracted refusal direction. The optimiser verifies candidates
      with an English keyword counter. Neither search reached the primary selection
      rule (&le; 10/100 keyword refusals); every candidate that a reference judge
      places below the selection threshold is invisible to the keyword objective
      (threshold-blind fraction 1.0). On 100 verified English-Slovene prompt pairs,
      the keyword counter fires on 87% of English responses and on 0% of Slovene
      responses, while the reference judge finds 13% English refusal and 82% Slovene
      refusal (<span class="num">&Delta;<sub>lang</sub> = &minus;1.56</span>, 95% CI
      [&minus;1.68, &minus;1.44]). Keyword-verified abliterated checkpoints are
      therefore not valid language-neutral references for refusal evaluation. The
      underlying edit itself transfers asymmetrically: GaMS3 Slovene refusal drops
      from 87% to 0%, but Gemma Slovene refusal drops only from 94% to 74%.
    </p>

    <div class="hero-links">
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/paper.pdf">Read the paper (PDF)</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/report.pdf" class="secondary">Read the full research report</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/exec_summary.pdf" class="secondary">Read the executive summary</a>
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses" class="secondary">Code repository</a>
    </div>
    <div class="round-links">
      Round reports:
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/round-1/report.pdf">Round 1</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/round-2/report.pdf">Round 2</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/round-3/report.pdf">Round 3</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/round-4/report.pdf">Round 4</a>
      <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/round-5/report.pdf">Round 5</a>
    </div>
  </section>

  <!-- CONTRIBUTIONS -->
  <section id="contributions">
    <h2>Contributions</h2>
    <div class="cards">
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Keyword measurement bias</h3>
        <p>
          The English keyword counter used by Heretic is silent on Slovene text: on 100
          verified Gemma-edit pairs it fires on 87% of English responses but 0% of Slovene responses,
          while the reference judge finds 82% Slovene refusal
          (&Delta;<sub>lang</sub> = &minus;1.56, 95% CI [&minus;1.68, &minus;1.44]).
          The threshold-blind fraction is 1.0 in both searches: counted by the keyword-based
          scorer C, 6/6 Gemma and 37/37 GaMS3 candidates below the threshold are invisible;
          the reference judge J confirms the pattern at 5/5 and 6/6. Keyword-verified
          abliterated checkpoints are not valid language-neutral references for refusal evaluation.
        </p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <h3>Depth placement: within-model signal, primary criterion falsified</h3>
        <p>
          Within each model, write-profile overlap correlates with residual refusal
          (GaMS3: &rho; = &minus;0.90; Gemma: &rho; = &minus;0.96 EN, &minus;0.83 SL),
          and replicates in Qwen3-8B (&rho; = &minus;0.76/&minus;0.93/&minus;0.84, 9/9 matched groups).
          The primary criterion, that placement explains variance beyond dose, was falsified
          (&Delta;R&sup2; = 0.027 and 0.056). At the keyword floor, dose dominates (p = 0.774).
          The frozen DEV index fails cross-model prediction (&rho; = &minus;0.009, n = 21, p = 0.16).
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </section>

  <!-- METHOD -->
  <section id="method">
    <h2>Method</h2>

    <h3>Models and checkpoints</h3>
    <p>
      Five checkpoints, all in 4-bit NF4 quantisation: <strong>Gemma-orig</strong>
      (<code>google/gemma-3-12b-it</code>), <strong>Gemma-edit</strong>
      (Heretic-optimised abliteration, 116 TPE trials, keyword objective),
      <strong>GaMS3-orig</strong> (<code>cjvt/GaMS3-12B-Instruct</code>, continually
      pretrained on Slovene), <strong>GaMS3-edit</strong> (same Heretic procedure),
      and a <strong>Community-ref</strong> (independently abliterated Gemma).
    </p>

    <h3>Heretic optimisation</h3>
    <p>
      Heretic uses tree-structured Parzen estimation (TPE) to search over abliteration
      hyperparameters: which layers to edit, the scaling coefficient, and the refusal-direction
      extraction method. It optimises two objectives: an English keyword refusal rate
      and KL divergence. The selection rule minimises KL subject to refusals &le; 10/100;
      if no candidate satisfies this, the fallback minimises refusals subject to KL &le; 1.0.
      Both searches fell to the fallback: no candidate achieved &le; 10 keyword refusals.
      The keyword objective floor was 72 for Gemma and 16 for GaMS3.
    </p>

    <h3>Evaluation protocol</h3>
    <p>
      All checkpoints are evaluated on the
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-1/dataset-1">RefusEU benchmark</a>:
      280 harmful prompts (S5 split) and 150 benign prompts (S6 split), each in English and Slovene.
      Responses are single greedy-decoded generations (temperature 0, max 256 tokens), classified
      into refused, partial, or complied by a local Qwen3-14B judge. Attack success rate (ASR)
      is computed where both Llama Guard 3 and PolyGuard agree. Over-refusal rate is the fraction
      of benign-prompt responses classified as refused.
    </p>
    <p>
      The 256-token limit truncates 94-95% of edited English outputs.
      The Qwen3-14B judge was calibrated against GPT-4.1: English &kappa; = 0.86 (gate met);
      Slovene &kappa; = 0.72 (gate not met). All Slovene absolute rates carry a measurement caveat.
      The depth-experiment judge also missed its gate (&kappa; = 0.683).
    </p>
  </section>

  <!-- RESULTS -->
  <section id="results">
    <h2>Results</h2>

    <h3>Refusal suppression across languages</h3>
    <p>
      Abliteration produces dramatically different cross-lingual outcomes for the two models.
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-2/experiment-4">Code: Bilingual safety test of four model versions.</a>
    </p>

    <div class="table-wrap">
      <table>
        <caption class="sr-only">Refusal rate, ASR, and over-refusal on RefusEU S5 harmful prompts (n=280 per cell), with 95% Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals.</caption>
        <thead>
          <tr><th>Checkpoint</th><th>Lang</th><th>Refusal</th><th>ASR</th><th>Over-refusal</th></tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td>GaMS3-orig</td><td>EN</td><td class="num">.986 [.971, .996]</td><td class="num">.015 [.004, .030]</td><td class="num">.100 [.053, .153]</td></tr>
          <tr><td>GaMS3-orig</td><td>SL</td><td class="num">.871 [.829, .907]</td><td class="num">.012 [.000, .027]</td><td class="num">.107 [.060, .160]</td></tr>
          <tr><td>GaMS3-edit</td><td>EN</td><td class="num">.014 [.004, .029]</td><td class="num">.982 [.964, .996]</td><td class="num">.000 [.000, .000]</td></tr>
          <tr><td>GaMS3-edit</td><td>SL</td><td class="num">.000 [.000, .000]</td><td class="num">.972 [.952, .992]</td><td class="num">.000 [.000, .000]</td></tr>
          <tr><td colspan="5" style="height:1px;padding:0;background:var(--c-border)"></td></tr>
          <tr><td>Gemma-orig</td><td>EN</td><td class="num">.971 [.950, .989]</td><td class="num">.026 [.007, .049]</td><td class="num">.087 [.040, .133]</td></tr>
          <tr><td>Gemma-orig</td><td>SL</td><td class="num">.939 [.911, .964]</td><td class="num">.016 [.004, .031]</td><td class="num">.327 [.253, .400]</td></tr>
          <tr><td>Gemma-edit</td><td>EN</td><td class="num">.287 [.233, .341]</td><td class="num">.738 [.681, .794]</td><td class="num">.013 [.000, .033]</td></tr>
          <tr><td>Gemma-edit</td><td>SL</td><td class="num">.739 [.686, .786]</td><td class="num">.103 [.067, .143]</td><td class="num">.193 [.133, .260]</td></tr>
          <tr><td colspan="5" style="height:1px;padding:0;background:var(--c-border)"></td></tr>
          <tr><td>Community-ref</td><td>EN</td><td class="num">.054 [.029, .082]</td><td class="num">1.00 [1.00, 1.00]</td><td class="num">.007 [.000, .020]</td></tr>
          <tr><td>Community-ref</td><td>SL</td><td class="num">.114 [.079, .154]</td><td class="num">.870 [.822, .909]</td><td class="num">.027 [.007, .053]</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>

    <p>
      <strong>GaMS3:</strong> abliteration removes refusal almost completely in both languages.
      English refusal drops from 98.6% to 1.4%; Slovene from 87.1% to 0.0%. The edit transfers fully.
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-2/experiment-6">Code: What English edits miss in Slovene: GaMS3 panel.</a>
    </p>
    <p>
      <strong>Gemma:</strong> abliteration partially suppresses English refusal
      (97.1% to 28.7%) but barely affects Slovene (93.9% to 73.9%).
      The English ASR reaches 73.8%, far below GaMS3's 98.2%; Slovene ASR is 10.3%.
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-2/experiment-7">Code: English edits barely unlock Slovene refusal in Gemma.</a>
    </p>
    <p>
      <strong>Community reference:</strong> the independently abliterated Gemma achieves much lower
      refusal in both English (5.4%) and Slovene (11.4%), suggesting that a more thorough abliteration
      procedure can reach deeper into the refusal mechanism.
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-1/experiment-1">Code: Same edit, very different safety effect.</a>
    </p>

    <h3>Keyword measurement bias</h3>

    <div class="result-highlight">
      <span class="big-num">&Delta;<sub>lang</sub> = &minus;1.56</span>
      The keyword counter fires on 87% of English responses but 0% of Slovene responses.
      The reference judge finds 13% English refusal and 82% Slovene refusal.
      95% CI [&minus;1.68, &minus;1.44].
    </div>

    <p>
      The keyword refusal counter counts English refusal phrases ("I cannot", "I'm sorry", etc.)
      in model responses. It is structurally unable to detect Slovene refusals.
      The threshold-blind fraction (TBF) is 1.0 in both searches: every candidate that
      a scorer places at or below the selection threshold (&le; 10/100 refusals) is invisible
      to the keyword objective. Under the keyword-based scorer C, 6/6 Gemma and 37/37 GaMS3
      candidates are invisible; under the reference judge J, 5/5 and 6/6.
      TBF = 1.0 follows from the keyword floors (72 for Gemma, 16 for GaMS3, both above the
      10-refusal threshold) and the counter's 81% false-positive rate on edited English text.
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-5/evaluation-5">Code: How blind is an English-only refusal score.</a>
    </p>

    <div class="table-wrap">
      <table>
        <caption class="sr-only">Keyword refusal counter vs. judge reference on held-out prompts.</caption>
        <thead>
          <tr><th>Condition</th><th>n</th><th>&kappa;</th><th>KW pos. rate</th><th>Ref. base rate</th><th>Mechanism</th></tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td>Original EN</td><td class="num">70</td><td class="num">0.20</td><td class="num">0.94</td><td class="num">0.94</td><td>CONCORDANT</td></tr>
          <tr><td>Original SL</td><td class="num">70</td><td class="num">0.00</td><td class="num">0.00</td><td class="num">0.96</td><td>SILENT</td></tr>
          <tr><td>Edited EN</td><td class="num">490</td><td class="num">0.02</td><td class="num">0.34</td><td class="num">0.17</td><td>MISFIRING</td></tr>
          <tr><td>Edited SL</td><td class="num">490</td><td class="num">0.00</td><td class="num">0.00</td><td class="num">0.44</td><td>SILENT</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>

    <p>
      On edited English text, 81% of the keyword counter's refusal detections are false positives,
      confirming that the counter both over-fires in English and is silent in Slovene.
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-4/experiment-15">Code: Can a refusal optimiser see its own refusals?</a>
    </p>

    <h3>Depth placement vs. dose</h3>

    <p>
      Heretic treats which layers to edit and the scaling coefficient as free parameters.
      We construct causal write profiles by applying single-layer abliteration edits in
      isolation, then measure residual refusal. The write-profile overlap
      O<sub>SL</sub> measures how well a multi-layer candidate concentrates energy on layers
      that matter.
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-4/experiment-13">Code: Where a refusal edit lands decides what survives.</a>
    </p>

    <p>
      For Gemma, Spearman correlations between write-profile overlap and residual refusal are
      &rho; = &minus;0.96 for English and &rho; = &minus;0.83 for Slovene (n = 18 weight cells).
      For GaMS3, &rho; = &minus;0.90 (Slovene, p &lt; 10<sup>&minus;7</sup>),
      holding at both energy levels (&rho; = &minus;0.97 at E2, &rho; = &minus;0.95 at E3).
      The overlap replicates in Qwen3-8B (&rho; = &minus;0.76 pooled, &minus;0.93 at E2,
      &minus;0.84 at E3, 9/9 matched groups).
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-4/experiment-14">Code: Where a refusal edit must land in a Slovene model.</a>
    </p>

    <div class="result-highlight">
      <span class="big-num">&Delta;R&sup2; = 0.027 / 0.056</span>
      Primary criterion falsified: placement does not explain variance in residual refusal beyond dose.
      At the keyword floor, dose dominates (p = 0.774). Raw depth alone does not predict residual
      refusal (&rho; = &minus;0.34, p = 0.15).
    </div>

    <p>
      The frozen activation-space DEV index fails cross-model prediction entirely:
      Spearman &rho; = &minus;0.009 over 21 pooled cells (95% CI [&minus;0.13, 0.19],
      permutation p = 0.16). The depth at which abliteration is most effective is model-specific;
      no fixed depth prescription carries from one model to another.
      <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-3/experiment-12">Code: Depth index fails to predict cross-lingual refusal-edit failure.</a>
    </p>
  </section>

  <!-- FIGURES -->
  <section id="figures">
    <h2>Figures</h2>
    <div class="figure-gallery">

      <figure class="figure-item">
        <div class="fig-img-wrap" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-label="Enlarge figure: Refusal Rates Before and After Abliteration" data-src="figures/fig_1_v0.png">
          <img src="figures/fig_1_v0.png" alt="Bar chart showing refusal rates on RefusEU S5 harmful prompts for five checkpoints in English and Slovene. GaMS3 edit drops to near zero in both languages, while Gemma edit drops only in English, remaining at 73.9% in Slovene." loading="lazy">
        </div>
        <figcaption>
          <strong>Figure 1: Refusal Rates Before and After Abliteration.</strong>
          Refusal rates on RefusEU S5 harmful prompts (n=280) for all five checkpoints. Bars are
          coloured by language: English (blue) and Slovene (orange). Abliteration transfers almost
          completely to Slovene for GaMS3 but fails for Gemma. The community reference checkpoint
          shows that deeper abliteration can partially overcome the language gap. Error bars show
          95% Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals. Note: 94-95% of edited English outputs were
          truncated at the 256-token generation limit.
        </figcaption>
      </figure>

      <figure class="figure-item">
        <div class="fig-img-wrap" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-label="Enlarge figure: Keyword Measurement Bias" data-src="figures/fig_2_v0.png">

        </div>
        <figcaption>
          <strong>Figure 2: Keyword Measurement Bias.</strong>
          Keyword counter vs. reference judge positive rates for the Gemma-edit checkpoint on 100
          verified paired prompts. The keyword counter fires on 87% of English responses but 0% of
          Slovene responses; the reference judge finds 13% English refusal and 82% Slovene refusal.
          &Delta;<sub>lang</sub> = d<sub>SL</sub> &minus; d<sub>EN</sub> = &minus;1.56
          [&minus;1.68, &minus;1.44]. The annotation shows TBF = 1.0: 6/6 Gemma and 37/37 GaMS3
          candidates invisible to the keyword objective are counted by scorer C; under judge J,
          the counts are 5/5 and 6/6.

          <img src="figures/fig_3_v0.png" alt="Two-panel scatter plot for GaMS3. Panel a shows residual Slovene refusal vs write-profile overlap with Spearman rho minus 0.90. Panel b shows residual refusal vs raw depth with rho minus 0.34, not significant." loading="lazy">
        </div>
        <figcaption>
          <strong>Figure 3: Depth Placement Profile for GaMS3.</strong>
          Residual Slovene refusal rate for GaMS3-12B-Instruct as a function of two predictors.
          (a) Write-profile overlap O<sub>SL</sub>: Spearman &rho; = &minus;0.90
          (p &lt; 10<sup>&minus;7</sup>); within energy levels,
          &rho; = &minus;0.97 (E2) and &rho; = &minus;0.95 (E3). Higher overlap with the causal
          write profile predicts lower residual refusal. (b) Raw depth of the edit (mean edited
          layer index): Spearman &rho; = &minus;0.34, p = 0.15 (not significant). Raw depth
          alone does not predict residual refusal; the overlap metric, which accounts for layer
          importance, is the informative predictor.

  <!-- LIMITATIONS -->
  <section id="limitations">
    <h2>Limitations</h2>
    <ul class="limitations-list">
      <li>
        <strong>Slovene judge certification.</strong> The Qwen3-14B workhorse judge does not meet
        the &kappa; &ge; 0.80 certification gate for Slovene (unweighted &kappa; = 0.72,
        CI [0.63, 0.81]). Absolute Slovene refusal rates may be biased. Within-Slovene relative
        comparisons are less affected.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong>Depth-experiment judge certification.</strong> The judge used in the depth-placement
        experiment also fails its certification gate (&kappa; = 0.683). The placement correlations
        carry this additional measurement caveat.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong>Generation truncation.</strong> 94-95% of edited English outputs and 70-92% of
        edited Slovene outputs were truncated at the 256-token generation limit. The judge classified
        refusal status from incomplete text.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong>Two models, one architecture.</strong> Both models are closely related (Gemma and
        its continual-pretraining derivative). The Qwen3-8B cross-model test provides one additional
        architecture, but a systematic survey across model families is needed.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong>One target language.</strong> Slovene is a mid-resource Indo-European language.
        The keyword measurement bias extends to any language the keyword counter does not cover,
        but the degree of edit transfer failure may differ for typologically distant or extremely
        low-resource languages.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong>NF4 quantisation.</strong> All experiments use 4-bit NF4 quantisation. The refusal
        direction and abliteration behaviour may differ at full precision.
      </li>
      <li>
        <strong>Single Heretic configuration.</strong> The abliteration uses a single Heretic
        configuration per model (116 TPE trials, default hyperparameter ranges). A more exhaustive
        search might yield different results.
      </li>
    </ul>
  </section>

(function() {
  "use strict";
  var overlay = document.getElementById("lightbox");
  var lbImg = document.getElementById("lightbox-img");
  var lbClose = document.getElementById("lightbox-close");
  var lastFocus = null;

  function openLightbox(src, alt) {
    lastFocus = document.activeElement;
    lbImg.src = src;
    lbImg.alt = alt || "";
    lbImg.style.display = "";
    overlay.classList.add("open");
    lbClose.focus();
    document.body.style.overflow = "hidden";
  }

  function closeLightbox() {
    overlay.classList.remove("open");
    lbImg.style.display = "none";
    document.body.style.overflow = "";
    if (lastFocus) lastFocus.focus();
  }

  var triggers = document.querySelectorAll(".fig-img-wrap[data-src]");
  for (var i = 0; i < triggers.length; i++) {
    (function(el) {
      el.addEventListener("click", function() {
        openLightbox(el.getAttribute("data-src"), el.querySelector("img").alt);
      });
      el.addEventListener("keydown", function(e) {
        if (e.key === "Enter" || e.key === " ") {
          e.preventDefault();
          openLightbox(el.getAttribute("data-src"), el.querySelector("img").alt);
        }
      });
    })(triggers[i]);
  }

  lbClose.addEventListener("click", closeLightbox);
  overlay.addEventListener("click", function(e) {
    if (e.target === overlay) closeLightbox();
  });
  document.addEventListener("keydown", function(e) {
    if (e.key === "Escape" && overlay.classList.contains("open")) closeLightbox();
  });
  overlay.addEventListener("keydown", function(e) {
    if (e.key === "Tab" && overlay.classList.contains("open")) {
      e.preventDefault(); lbClose.focus();
    }
  });

  var navLinks = document.querySelectorAll("nav.section-nav a");
  var sections = [];
  for (var j = 0; j < navLinks.length; j++) {
    var id = navLinks[j].getAttribute("href").substring(1);
    var sec = document.getElementById(id);
    if (sec) sections.push({ el: sec, link: navLinks[j] });
  }
  function updateNav() {
    var scrollY = window.scrollY + 120;
    var current = null;
    for (var k = 0; k < sections.length; k++) {
      if (sections[k].el.offsetTop <= scrollY) current = k;
    }
    for (var m = 0; m < sections.length; m++) {
      sections[m].link.classList.toggle("active", m === current);
    }
  }
  var ticking = false;
  window.addEventListener("scroll", function() {
    if (!ticking) {
      requestAnimationFrame(function() { updateNav(); ticking = false; });
      ticking = true;
    }
  }, { passive: true });
  updateNav();
})();
</script>

animation-duration: 0s !important;\n  }\n}\n@media print {\n  nav.section-nav { display: none; }\n  .lightbox-overlay { display: none !important; }\n}\n</style>\n</head>\n<body>\n\n<a class=\"skip-link\" href=\"#main-content\">Skip to main content</a>\n\n<nav class=\"section-nav\" aria-label=\"Section navigation\">\n  <ol>\n    <li><a href=\"#hero\">Overview</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#contributions\">Contributions</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#method\">Method</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#results\">Results</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#figures\">Figures</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#limitations\">Limitations</a></li>\n  </ol>\n</nav>\n\n<main id=\"main-content\">\n\n  <!-- HERO -->\n  <section class=\"hero\" id=\"hero\">\n    <h1>An English Keyword Objective Is Blind to Its Own Edit in Slovene</h1>\n\n    <p class=\"tldr\">\n      Abliteration removes refusal from language models by orthogonalising weights\n      against an English-extracted refusal direction. The optimiser verifies candidates\n      with an English keyword counter. Neither search reached the primary selection\n      rule (&le; 10/100 keyword refusals); every candidate that a reference judge\n      places below the selection threshold is invisible to the keyword objective\n      (threshold-blind fraction 1.0). On 100 verified English-Slovene prompt pairs,\n      the keyword counter fires on 87% of English responses and on 0% of Slovene\n      responses, while the reference judge finds 13% English refusal and 82% Slovene\n      refusal (<span class=\"num\">&Delta;<sub>lang</sub> = &minus;1.56</span>, 95% CI\n      [&minus;1.68, &minus;1.44]). Keyword-verified abliterated checkpoints are\n      therefore not valid language-neutral references for refusal evaluation. The\n      underlying edit itself transfers asymmetrically: GaMS3 Slovene refusal drops\n      from 87% to 0%, but Gemma Slovene refusal drops only from 94% to 74%.\n    </p>\n\n    <div class=\"hero-links\">\n      <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/paper.pdf\">Read the paper (PDF)</a>\n      <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/report.pdf\" class=\"secondary\">Read the full research report</a>\n      <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/exec_summary.pdf\" class=\"secondary\">Read the executive summary</a>\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses\" class=\"secondary\">Code repository</a>\n    </div>\n    <div class=\"round-links\">\n      Round reports:\n      <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/round-1/report.pdf\">Round 1</a>\n      <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/round-2/report.pdf\">Round 2</a>\n      <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/round-3/report.pdf\">Round 3</a>\n      <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/round-4/report.pdf\">Round 4</a>\n      <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses@main/round-5/report.pdf\">Round 5</a>\n    </div>\n  </section>\n\n  <!-- CONTRIBUTIONS -->\n  <section id=\"contributions\">\n    <h2>Contributions</h2>\n    <div class=\"cards\">\n      <div class=\"card\">\n        <h3>Keyword measurement bias</h3>\n        <p>\n          The English keyword counter used by Heretic is silent on Slovene text: on 100\n          verified Gemma-edit pairs it fires on 87% of English responses but 0% of Slovene responses,\n          while the reference judge finds 82% Slovene refusal\n          (&Delta;<sub>lang</sub> = &minus;1.56, 95% CI [&minus;1.68, &minus;1.44]).\n          The threshold-blind fraction is 1.0 in both searches: counted by the keyword-based\n          scorer C, 6/6 Gemma and 37/37 GaMS3 candidates below the threshold are invisible;\n          the reference judge J confirms the pattern at 5/5 and 6/6. Keyword-verified\n          abliterated checkpoints are not valid language-neutral references for refusal evaluation.\n        </p>\n      </div>\n      <div class=\"card\">\n        <h3>Depth placement: within-model signal, primary criterion falsified</h3>\n        <p>\n          Within each model, write-profile overlap correlates with residual refusal\n          (GaMS3: &rho; = &minus;0.90; Gemma: &rho; = &minus;0.96 EN, &minus;0.83 SL),\n          and replicates in Qwen3-8B (&rho; = &minus;0.76/&minus;0.93/&minus;0.84, 9/9 matched groups).\n          The primary criterion, that placement explains variance beyond dose, was falsified\n          (&Delta;R&sup2; = 0.027 and 0.056). At the keyword floor, dose dominates (p = 0.774).\n          The frozen DEV index fails cross-model prediction (&rho; = &minus;0.009, n = 21, p = 0.16).\n        </p>\n      </div>\n    </div>\n  </section>\n\n  <!-- METHOD -->\n  <section id=\"method\">\n    <h2>Method</h2>\n\n    <h3>Models and checkpoints</h3>\n    <p>\n      Five checkpoints, all in 4-bit NF4 quantisation: <strong>Gemma-orig</strong>\n      (<code>google/gemma-3-12b-it</code>), <strong>Gemma-edit</strong>\n      (Heretic-optimised abliteration, 116 TPE trials, keyword objective),\n      <strong>GaMS3-orig</strong> (<code>cjvt/GaMS3-12B-Instruct</code>, continually\n      pretrained on Slovene), <strong>GaMS3-edit</strong> (same Heretic procedure),\n      and a <strong>Community-ref</strong> (independently abliterated Gemma).\n    </p>\n\n    <h3>Heretic optimisation</h3>\n    <p>\n      Heretic uses tree-structured Parzen estimation (TPE) to search over abliteration\n      hyperparameters: which layers to edit, the scaling coefficient, and the refusal-direction\n      extraction method. It optimises two objectives: an English keyword refusal rate\n      and KL divergence. The selection rule minimises KL subject to refusals &le; 10/100;\n      if no candidate satisfies this, the fallback minimises refusals subject to KL &le; 1.0.\n      Both searches fell to the fallback: no candidate achieved &le; 10 keyword refusals.\n      The keyword objective floor was 72 for Gemma and 16 for GaMS3.\n    </p>\n\n    <h3>Evaluation protocol</h3>\n    <p>\n      All checkpoints are evaluated on the\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-1/dataset-1\">RefusEU benchmark</a>:\n      280 harmful prompts (S5 split) and 150 benign prompts (S6 split), each in English and Slovene.\n      Responses are single greedy-decoded generations (temperature 0, max 256 tokens), classified\n      into refused, partial, or complied by a local Qwen3-14B judge. Attack success rate (ASR)\n      is computed where both Llama Guard 3 and PolyGuard agree. Over-refusal rate is the fraction\n      of benign-prompt responses classified as refused.\n    </p>\n    <p>\n      The 256-token limit truncates 94-95% of edited English outputs.\n      The Qwen3-14B judge was calibrated against GPT-4.1: English &kappa; = 0.86 (gate met);\n      Slovene &kappa; = 0.72 (gate not met). All Slovene absolute rates carry a measurement caveat.\n      The depth-experiment judge also missed its gate (&kappa; = 0.683).\n    </p>\n  </section>\n\n  <!-- RESULTS -->\n  <section id=\"results\">\n    <h2>Results</h2>\n\n    <h3>Refusal suppression across languages</h3>\n    <p>\n      Abliteration produces dramatically different cross-lingual outcomes for the two models.\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-2/experiment-4\">Code: Bilingual safety test of four model versions.</a>\n    </p>\n\n    <div class=\"table-wrap\">\n      <table>\n        <caption class=\"sr-only\">Refusal rate, ASR, and over-refusal on RefusEU S5 harmful prompts (n=280 per cell), with 95% Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals.</caption>\n        <thead>\n          <tr><th>Checkpoint</th><th>Lang</th><th>Refusal</th><th>ASR</th><th>Over-refusal</th></tr>\n        </thead>\n        <tbody>\n          <tr><td>GaMS3-orig</td><td>EN</td><td class=\"num\">.986 [.971, .996]</td><td class=\"num\">.015 [.004, .030]</td><td class=\"num\">.100 [.053, .153]</td></tr>\n          <tr><td>GaMS3-orig</td><td>SL</td><td class=\"num\">.871 [.829, .907]</td><td class=\"num\">.012 [.000, .027]</td><td class=\"num\">.107 [.060, .160]</td></tr>\n          <tr><td>GaMS3-edit</td><td>EN</td><td class=\"num\">.014 [.004, .029]</td><td class=\"num\">.982 [.964, .996]</td><td class=\"num\">.000 [.000, .000]</td></tr>\n          <tr><td>GaMS3-edit</td><td>SL</td><td class=\"num\">.000 [.000, .000]</td><td class=\"num\">.972 [.952, .992]</td><td class=\"num\">.000 [.000, .000]</td></tr>\n          <tr><td colspan=\"5\" style=\"height:1px;padding:0;background:var(--c-border)\"></td></tr>\n          <tr><td>Gemma-orig</td><td>EN</td><td class=\"num\">.971 [.950, .989]</td><td class=\"num\">.026 [.007, .049]</td><td class=\"num\">.087 [.040, .133]</td></tr>\n          <tr><td>Gemma-orig</td><td>SL</td><td class=\"num\">.939 [.911, .964]</td><td class=\"num\">.016 [.004, .031]</td><td class=\"num\">.327 [.253, .400]</td></tr>\n          <tr><td>Gemma-edit</td><td>EN</td><td class=\"num\">.287 [.233, .341]</td><td class=\"num\">.738 [.681, .794]</td><td class=\"num\">.013 [.000, .033]</td></tr>\n          <tr><td>Gemma-edit</td><td>SL</td><td class=\"num\">.739 [.686, .786]</td><td class=\"num\">.103 [.067, .143]</td><td class=\"num\">.193 [.133, .260]</td></tr>\n          <tr><td colspan=\"5\" style=\"height:1px;padding:0;background:var(--c-border)\"></td></tr>\n          <tr><td>Community-ref</td><td>EN</td><td class=\"num\">.054 [.029, .082]</td><td class=\"num\">1.00 [1.00, 1.00]</td><td class=\"num\">.007 [.000, .020]</td></tr>\n          <tr><td>Community-ref</td><td>SL</td><td class=\"num\">.114 [.079, .154]</td><td class=\"num\">.870 [.822, .909]</td><td class=\"num\">.027 [.007, .053]</td></tr>\n        </tbody>\n      </table>\n    </div>\n\n    <p>\n      <strong>GaMS3:</strong> abliteration removes refusal almost completely in both languages.\n      English refusal drops from 98.6% to 1.4%; Slovene from 87.1% to 0.0%. The edit transfers fully.\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-2/experiment-6\">Code: What English edits miss in Slovene: GaMS3 panel.</a>\n    </p>\n    <p>\n      <strong>Gemma:</strong> abliteration partially suppresses English refusal\n      (97.1% to 28.7%) but barely affects Slovene (93.9% to 73.9%).\n      The English ASR reaches 73.8%, far below GaMS3's 98.2%; Slovene ASR is 10.3%.\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-2/experiment-7\">Code: English edits barely unlock Slovene refusal in Gemma.</a>\n    </p>\n    <p>\n      <strong>Community reference:</strong> the independently abliterated Gemma achieves much lower\n      refusal in both English (5.4%) and Slovene (11.4%), suggesting that a more thorough abliteration\n      procedure can reach deeper into the refusal mechanism.\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-1/experiment-1\">Code: Same edit, very different safety effect.</a>\n    </p>\n\n    <h3>Keyword measurement bias</h3>\n\n    <div class=\"result-highlight\">\n      <span class=\"big-num\">&Delta;<sub>lang</sub> = &minus;1.56</span>\n      The keyword counter fires on 87% of English responses but 0% of Slovene responses.\n      The reference judge finds 13% English refusal and 82% Slovene refusal.\n      95% CI [&minus;1.68, &minus;1.44].\n    </div>\n\n    <p>\n      The keyword refusal counter counts English refusal phrases (\"I cannot\", \"I'm sorry\", etc.)\n      in model responses. It is structurally unable to detect Slovene refusals.\n      The threshold-blind fraction (TBF) is 1.0 in both searches: every candidate that\n      a scorer places at or below the selection threshold (&le; 10/100 refusals) is invisible\n      to the keyword objective. Under the keyword-based scorer C, 6/6 Gemma and 37/37 GaMS3\n      candidates are invisible; under the reference judge J, 5/5 and 6/6.\n      TBF = 1.0 follows from the keyword floors (72 for Gemma, 16 for GaMS3, both above the\n      10-refusal threshold) and the counter's 81% false-positive rate on edited English text.\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-5/evaluation-5\">Code: How blind is an English-only refusal score.</a>\n    </p>\n\n    <div class=\"table-wrap\">\n      <table>\n        <caption class=\"sr-only\">Keyword refusal counter vs. judge reference on held-out prompts.</caption>\n        <thead>\n          <tr><th>Condition</th><th>n</th><th>&kappa;</th><th>KW pos. rate</th><th>Ref. base rate</th><th>Mechanism</th></tr>\n        </thead>\n        <tbody>\n          <tr><td>Original EN</td><td class=\"num\">70</td><td class=\"num\">0.20</td><td class=\"num\">0.94</td><td class=\"num\">0.94</td><td>CONCORDANT</td></tr>\n          <tr><td>Original SL</td><td class=\"num\">70</td><td class=\"num\">0.00</td><td class=\"num\">0.00</td><td class=\"num\">0.96</td><td>SILENT</td></tr>\n          <tr><td>Edited EN</td><td class=\"num\">490</td><td class=\"num\">0.02</td><td class=\"num\">0.34</td><td class=\"num\">0.17</td><td>MISFIRING</td></tr>\n          <tr><td>Edited SL</td><td class=\"num\">490</td><td class=\"num\">0.00</td><td class=\"num\">0.00</td><td class=\"num\">0.44</td><td>SILENT</td></tr>\n        </tbody>\n      </table>\n    </div>\n\n    <p>\n      On edited English text, 81% of the keyword counter's refusal detections are false positives,\n      confirming that the counter both over-fires in English and is silent in Slovene.\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-4/experiment-15\">Code: Can a refusal optimiser see its own refusals?</a>\n    </p>\n\n    <h3>Depth placement vs. dose</h3>\n\n    <p>\n      Heretic treats which layers to edit and the scaling coefficient as free parameters.\n      We construct causal write profiles by applying single-layer abliteration edits in\n      isolation, then measure residual refusal. The write-profile overlap\n      O<sub>SL</sub> measures how well a multi-layer candidate concentrates energy on layers\n      that matter.\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-4/experiment-13\">Code: Where a refusal edit lands decides what survives.</a>\n    </p>\n\n    <p>\n      For Gemma, Spearman correlations between write-profile overlap and residual refusal are\n      &rho; = &minus;0.96 for English and &rho; = &minus;0.83 for Slovene (n = 18 weight cells).\n      For GaMS3, &rho; = &minus;0.90 (Slovene, p &lt; 10<sup>&minus;7</sup>),\n      holding at both energy levels (&rho; = &minus;0.97 at E2, &rho; = &minus;0.95 at E3).\n      The overlap replicates in Qwen3-8B (&rho; = &minus;0.76 pooled, &minus;0.93 at E2,\n      &minus;0.84 at E3, 9/9 matched groups).\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-4/experiment-14\">Code: Where a refusal edit must land in a Slovene model.</a>\n    </p>\n\n    <div class=\"result-highlight\">\n      <span class=\"big-num\">&Delta;R&sup2; = 0.027 / 0.056</span>\n      Primary criterion falsified: placement does not explain variance in residual refusal beyond dose.\n      At the keyword floor, dose dominates (p = 0.774). Raw depth alone does not predict residual\n      refusal (&rho; = &minus;0.34, p = 0.15).\n    </div>\n\n    <p>\n      The frozen activation-space DEV index fails cross-model prediction entirely:\n      Spearman &rho; = &minus;0.009 over 21 pooled cells (95% CI [&minus;0.13, 0.19],\n      permutation p = 0.16). The depth at which abliteration is most effective is model-specific;\n      no fixed depth prescription carries from one model to another.\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-3/experiment-12\">Code: Depth index fails to predict cross-lingual refusal-edit failure.</a>\n    </p>\n  </section>\n\n  <!-- FIGURES -->\n  <section id=\"figures\">\n    <h2>Figures</h2>\n    <div class=\"figure-gallery\">\n\n      <figure class=\"figure-item\">\n        <div class=\"fig-img-wrap\" role=\"button\" tabindex=\"0\" aria-label=\"Enlarge figure: Refusal Rates Before and After Abliteration\" data-src=\"figures/fig_1_v0.png\">\n          <img src=\"figures/fig_1_v0.png\" alt=\"Bar chart showing refusal rates on RefusEU S5 harmful prompts for five checkpoints in English and Slovene. GaMS3 edit drops to near zero in both languages, while Gemma edit drops only in English, remaining at 73.9% in Slovene.\" loading=\"lazy\">\n        </div>\n        <figcaption>\n          <strong>Figure 1: Refusal Rates Before and After Abliteration.</strong>\n          Refusal rates on RefusEU S5 harmful prompts (n=280) for all five checkpoints. Bars are\n          coloured by language: English (blue) and Slovene (orange). Abliteration transfers almost\n          completely to Slovene for GaMS3 but fails for Gemma. The community reference checkpoint\n          shows that deeper abliteration can partially overcome the language gap. Error bars show\n          95% Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals. Note: 94-95% of edited English outputs were\n          truncated at the 256-token generation limit.\n        </figcaption>\n      </figure>\n\n      <figure class=\"figure-item\">\n        <div class=\"fig-img-wrap\" role=\"button\" tabindex=\"0\" aria-label=\"Enlarge figure: Keyword Measurement Bias\" data-src=\"figures/fig_2_v0.png\">\n          <img src=\"figures/fig_2_v0.png\" alt=\"Side-by-side bar charts comparing keyword counter vs reference judge positive rates. The keyword counter fires on 87% of English but 0% of Slovene responses; the reference judge finds 13% English and 82% Slovene refusal.\" loading=\"lazy\">\n        </div>\n        <figcaption>\n          <strong>Figure 2: Keyword Measurement Bias.</strong>\n          Keyword counter vs. reference judge positive rates for the Gemma-edit checkpoint on 100\n          verified paired prompts. The keyword counter fires on 87% of English responses but 0% of\n          Slovene responses; the reference judge finds 13% English refusal and 82% Slovene refusal.\n          &Delta;<sub>lang</sub> = d<sub>SL</sub> &minus; d<sub>EN</sub> = &minus;1.56\n          [&minus;1.68, &minus;1.44]. The annotation shows TBF = 1.0: 6/6 Gemma and 37/37 GaMS3\n          candidates invisible to the keyword objective are counted by scorer C; under judge J,\n          the counts are 5/5 and 6/6.\n        </figcaption>\n      </figure>\n\n      <figure class=\"figure-item\">\n        <div class=\"fig-img-wrap\" role=\"button\" tabindex=\"0\" aria-label=\"Enlarge figure: Depth Placement Profile for GaMS3\" data-src=\"figures/fig_3_v0.png\">\n          <img src=\"figures/fig_3_v0.png\" alt=\"Two-panel scatter plot for GaMS3. Panel a shows residual Slovene refusal vs write-profile overlap with Spearman rho minus 0.90. Panel b shows residual refusal vs raw depth with rho minus 0.34, not significant.\" loading=\"lazy\">\n        </div>\n        <figcaption>\n          <strong>Figure 3: Depth Placement Profile for GaMS3.</strong>\n          Residual Slovene refusal rate for GaMS3-12B-Instruct as a function of two predictors.\n          (a) Write-profile overlap O<sub>SL</sub>: Spearman &rho; = &minus;0.90\n          (p &lt; 10<sup>&minus;7</sup>); within energy levels,\n          &rho; = &minus;0.97 (E2) and &rho; = &minus;0.95 (E3). Higher overlap with the causal\n          write profile predicts lower residual refusal. (b) Raw depth of the edit (mean edited\n          layer index): Spearman &rho; = &minus;0.34, p = 0.15 (not significant). Raw depth\n          alone does not predict residual refusal; the overlap metric, which accounts for layer\n          importance, is the informative predictor.\n        </figcaption>\n      </figure>\n\n    </div>\n  </section>\n\n  <!-- LIMITATIONS -->\n  <section id=\"limitations\">\n    <h2>Limitations</h2>\n    <ul class=\"limitations-list\">\n      <li>\n        <strong>Slovene judge certification.</strong> The Qwen3-14B workhorse judge does not meet\n        the &kappa; &ge; 0.80 certification gate for Slovene (unweighted &kappa; = 0.72,\n        CI [0.63, 0.81]). Absolute Slovene refusal rates may be biased. Within-Slovene relative\n        comparisons are less affected.\n      </li>\n      <li>\n        <strong>Depth-experiment judge certification.</strong> The judge used in the depth-placement\n        experiment also fails its certification gate (&kappa; = 0.683). The placement correlations\n        carry this additional measurement caveat.\n      </li>\n      <li>\n        <strong>Generation truncation.</strong> 94-95% of edited English outputs and 70-92% of\n        edited Slovene outputs were truncated at the 256-token generation limit. The judge classified\n        refusal status from incomplete text.\n      </li>\n      <li>\n        <strong>Two models, one architecture.</strong> Both models are closely related (Gemma and\n        its continual-pretraining derivative). The Qwen3-8B cross-model test provides one additional\n        architecture, but a systematic survey across model families is needed.\n      </li>\n      <li>\n        <strong>One target language.</strong> Slovene is a mid-resource Indo-European language.\n        The keyword measurement bias extends to any language the keyword counter does not cover,\n        but the degree of edit transfer failure may differ for typologically distant or extremely\n        low-resource languages.\n      </li>\n      <li>\n        <strong>NF4 quantisation.</strong> All experiments use 4-bit NF4 quantisation. The refusal\n        direction and abliteration behaviour may differ at full precision.\n      </li>\n      <li>\n        <strong>Single Heretic configuration.</strong> The abliteration uses a single Heretic\n        configuration per model (116 TPE trials, default hyperparameter ranges). A more exhaustive\n        search might yield different results.\n      </li>\n    </ul>\n  </section>\n\n  <!-- CODE ARTIFACTS -->\n  <section class=\"code-artifacts\" id=\"code-list\">\n    <h2>Experiment code</h2>\n    <ul>\n      <li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-1/experiment-1\">Same edit, very different safety effect</a></li>\n      <li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-1/experiment-3\">English vs Slovene refusal-direction transfer test</a></li>\n      <li><a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-1/dataset-1\">Frozen English/Slovene safety and utility test sets</a></li>\n The optimiser verifies candidates\n      with an English keyword counter. Neither search reached the primary selection\n      rule (&le; 10/100 keyword refusals); every candidate that a reference judge\n      places below the selection threshold is invisible to the keyword objective\n      (threshold-blind fraction 1.0). On 100 verified English-Slovene prompt pairs,\n      the keyword counter fires on 87% of English responses and on 0% of Slovene\n      responses, while the reference judge finds 13% English refusal and 82% Slovene\n      refusal (<span class=\"num\">&Delta;<sub>lang</sub> = &minus;1.56</span>, 95% CI\n      [&minus;1.68, &minus;1.44]). Keyword-verified abliterated checkpoints are\n      therefore not valid language-neutral references for refusal evaluation. The\n      underlying edit itself transfers asymmetrically: GaMS3 Slovene refusal drops\n      from 87% to 0%, but Gemma Slovene refusal drops only from 94% to 74%.\n    </p>\n\n    <div -->\n  <section id=\"contributions\">\n    <h2>Contributions</h2>\n    <div class=\"cards\">\n      <div class=\"card\">\n        <h3>Keyword measurement bias</h3>\n        <p>\n          The English keyword counter used by Heretic is silent on Slovene text: on 100\n          verified Gemma-edit pairs it fires on 87% of English responses but 0% of Slovene responses,\n          while the reference judge finds 82% Slovene refusal\n          (&Delta;<sub>lang</sub> = &minus;1.56, 95% CI [&minus;1.68, &minus;1.44]).\n          The threshold-blind fraction is 1.0 in both searches: counted by the keyword-based\n          scorer C, 6/6 Gemma and 37/37 GaMS3 candidates below the threshold are invisible;\n          the reference judge J confirms the pattern at 5/5 and 6/6. Keyword-verified\n          abliterated checkpoints are not valid language-neutral references for refusal evaluation.\n        </p>\n      </div>\n      <div class=\"card\">\n        <h3>Depth placement: within-model signal, primary criterion falsified</h3>\n        <p>\n          Within each model, write-profile overlap correlates with residual refusal\n          (GaMS3: &rho; = &minus;0.90; Gemma: &rho; = &minus;0.96 EN, &minus;0.83 SL),\n          and replicates in Qwen3-8B (&rho; = &minus;0.76/&minus;0.93/&minus;0.84, 9/9 matched groups).\n          The primary criterion, that placement explains variance beyond dose, was falsified\n          (&Delta;R&sup2; = 0.027 and 0.056). At the keyword floor, dose dominates (p = 0.774).\n          The frozen DEV index fails cross-model prediction (&rho; = &minus;0.009, n = 21, p = 0.16).\n        </p>\n      </div>\n    </div>\n  </section>\n\n  <!-- METHOD -->\n  <section id=\"method\">\n    <h2>Method</h2>\n\n    <h3>Models and checkpoints</h3>\n    <p>\n      Five checkpoints, all in 4-bit NF4 quantisation: <strong>Gemma-orig</strong>\n      (<code>google/gemma-3-12b-it</code>), <strong>Gemma-edit</strong>\n      (Heretic-optimised abliteration, 116 TPE trials, keyword objective),\n      <strong>GaMS3-orig</strong> (<code>cjvt/GaMS3-12B-Instruct</code>, continually\n      pretrained on Slovene), <strong>GaMS3-edit</strong> (same Heretic procedure),\n      and a <strong>Community-ref</strong> (independently abliterated Gemma).\n    </p>\n\n    <h3>Heretic optimisation</h3>\n    <p>\n      Heretic uses tree-structured Parzen estimation (TPE) to search over abliteration\n      hyperparameters: which layers to edit, the scaling coefficient, and the refusal-direction\n      extraction method. It optimises two objectives: an English keyword refusal rate\n      and KL divergence. The selection rule minimises KL subject to refusals &le; 10/100;\n      if no candidate satisfies this, the fallback minimises refusals subject to KL &le; 1.0.\n      Both searches fell to the fallback: no candidate achieved &le; 10 keyword refusals.\n      The keyword objective floor was 72 for Gemma and 16 for GaMS3.\n    </p>\n\n    <h3>Evaluation protocol</h3>\n    <p>\n      All checkpoints are evaluated on the\n      <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-beaa2a-what-english-tuned-abliteration-misses/tree/main/round-1/dataset-1\">RefusEU benchmark</a>:\n      280 harmful prompts (S5 split) and 150 benign prompts (S6 split), each in English and Slovene.\n      Responses are single greedy-decoded generations (temperature 0, max 256 tokens), classified\n      into refused, partial, or complied by a local Qwen3-14B judge. Attack success rate (ASR)\n      is computed where both Llama Guard 3 and PolyGuard agree. Over-refusal rate is the fraction\n      of benign-prompt responses classified as refused.\n    </p>\n    <p>\n      The 256-token limit truncates 94-95% of edited English outputs.\n      The Qwen3-14B judge was calibrated against GPT-4.1: English &kappa; = 0.86 (gate met);\n      Slovene &kappa; = 0.72 (gate not met). All Slovene absolute rates carry a measurement caveat.\n      The depth-experiment judge also missed its gate (&kappa; = 0.683).\n    </p>\n  </section>\n\n  <!-- RESULTS -->\n  <section
